title: Brand: Managing Training Data with Batched Random Access
summary:
This paper propose Brand, a comprehensive memory management system for deep
learning training (DLT) where the memory capacity is much smaller than the size
of the training datasets. Brand starts with a bold design choice that data
files are always read from disk in batch, named chunk. Based on this
assumption, we propose efficient data access protocol in both single-node
setting and distributed environment with multiple nodes. The protocol minimizes
the wasted data read due to larger granularity, enables efficient inter-node
prefetching, while still ensuring randomness required by DLT. The experimental
results indicate that Brand can significantly accelerate data fetching in DLT,
achieving up to a 4.57x improvement in end-to-end training compared to PyTorch.

\subsection*{Abstract}
This paper propose Brand, a comprehensive memory management system for deep learning training (DLT) 
where the memory capacity is 
much smaller than the size of the training datasets.
Brand starts with a bold design choice that 
data files are {\em always} read from disk in batch,
named {\em chunk}.
Based on this assumption, we propose efficient
data access protocol in both single-node
setting and distributed environment with multiple
nodes. 
The protocol minimizes the wasted data read
due to larger granularity, enables efficient
inter-node prefetching, while still ensuring 
\xuehai{{\em randomness}} required by DLT. The experimental results indicate that Brand can significantly accelerate data fetching in DLT, achieving up to a 4.57x improvement in end-to-end training compared to PyTorch. 

\section{Introduction}

\label{sec:introduction}
 \textit{Deep Learning} (DL)~\cite{lecun2015deeplearning,schmidhuber2015deepneuralnetworks}  has permeated various domains, including computer vision~\cite{krizhevsky2012alexnet,he2016resnet,howard2017mobilenets}, speech recognition~\cite{hinton2012speech,graves2013speech,amodei2016speech}, and natural language processing~\cite{mikolov2013nlp,vaswani2017attentionnlp,devlin2018bertnlp}, becoming ubiquitous in the society. The widespread adoption of DL can be largely attributed to its remarkable accuracy, a quality dependent on not only the \textit{Deep Neural Network} (DNN) algorithms but also the training dataset. 
 %The algorithm plays a crucial role in determining the depth of the model by defining its structure and complexity. 
 %Meanwhile, the dataset contributes to the model's breadth by providing a rich foundation of information for learning. For dataset, 
 Datasets with high quality, rich diversity, and large quantity 
 %contribute to great effectiveness 
 are crucial in achieving high accuracy of DNN models. As a result, the datasets used for training DNN models are growing increasingly larger. For instance, Open Images~\cite{kuznetsova2020openimages} is a dataset with millions of entries, exceeding 500 GB in size, while ImageNet-21k~\cite{deng2009imagenet} is even larger at 1.1 TB, encompassing tens of millions of data instances. 
 Such massive-scale datasets will impose significant I/O pressure on \textit{Deep Learning Training} (DLT). 
\xuehai{In particular, the importance of I/O
performance bottleneck
is exaggerated by the profound
advance of high-performance 
{\em computation} accelerators, e.g., GPUs and TPUs~\cite{jouppi2017TPU}), which 
further increases the gap between the speed
to process training data and to get 
data out of disk~\cite{mohan2021coordl,khan2023shade,kumar2020quiver}. }
 
% In particular, given the advancement of high-performance computation accelerators, e.g., GPUs and TPUs~\cite{jouppi2017TPU}), being able to speed up the computation part of DLT significantly, I/O has emerged as a new performance bottleneck~\cite{mohan2021coordl,khan2023shade,kumar2020quiver}. 


Solving DLT's I/O bottleneck faces two challenges.  
The first one is the large and \xuehai{{\em ever-growing}} 
training data.
The huge gap between the processing 
speed of compute units such as CPUs/GPUs and 
the I/O performance is well known.
%In many applications, such gap can be mitigated by 
\xuehai{The conventional way to close the gap is to 
leverage}
the basic principle of memory hierarchy:
leveraging memory 
as a layer between I/O and compute units.
However, the huge size of the training data---crucial
to achieve high model accuracy---only allow memory
to keep a small portion of the data. 
Intelligent memory management mechanisms 
can typically enable efficient data caching~\cite{patterson2016computerorganization}, 
but such capability is hindered by the second challenge:
the access pattern
for DLT is \xuehai{{\em completely}} random.
This makes various replacement policies, such as Least Recently Used (LRU) or Least Frequently Used (LFU), aiming to capture certain access patterns, obsolete. 
DLT randomly iterates over training dataset \xuehai{during} each epoch, and such randomness is required to 
ensure training efficiency. 
%This characteristic renders the existing data 
%replacement policies ineffective. 




%this is not achievable in DLT when the size of the dataset far exceeds the memory capacity. 
%The ideal scenario is that all data requests from the DL framework can retrieve data directly from memory. However, this is not achievable in DLT when the size of the dataset far exceeds the memory capacity.
%This is because DLT iterates over the large dataset following a random access sequence for each epoch, which means that each data in the dataset will be processed at an uncertain time during each epoch. 

%Such a random data access pattern poses a significant challenge to memory management, making it difficult to achieve high memory hit rate using typical memory replacement strategies in operating systems, such as LRU and LFU. 
%Once a memory miss occurs, the DL framework needs to wait to retrieve data from the storage, making the I/O a bottleneck. 

Due to \xuehai{the} random access pattern, 
the design and optimization space for DLT data's memory 
management is very limited. 
Without affecting randomness, 
most existing methods~\cite{mohan2021coordl, yang2019locality-aware, dryden2021nopfs} cache
a fixed portion of data in memory, enabling faster
access for the cached data while \xuehai{still} incurring
high latency for the uncached data through I/O. 
Based \yuhao{on} such static caching policy, 
the proportion of data access that can be 
accelerated depends entirely on the memory capacity \xuehai{which, unfortunately}, 
does \xuehai{not} scale with the data amount. 
%Given the increasing DLT data sizes,
%the capacity gap between the size of DLT data sets 
%and memory will continue to grow, leading to the 
%diminishing benefits of the cached data. 
Thus, significantly improving the efficiency
of DLT data access requires fundamental innovation.
%rather than relying on existing caching mechanisms
%that are designed for different application domains.
%This paper makes the first attempt in this direction. 

To develop a new solution from ground up, 
we start with \xuehai{the fundamental DLT data 
access properties involving 
four key characteristics}:
(1) \xuehai{\em completely random}---required to 
ensure the training efficiency;
(2) {\em no \xuehai{unique} accessing order}---\xuehai{providing
unique system optimization opportunity}; 
(3) {\em variable} data access granularity---read
data files containing training data of different sizes;
(4) {\em ``access-once''}---a data file is only accessed once per iteration. 
The four characteristics pose significant challenges
for the \xuehai{conventional} cache designs that explore
the temporal and spatial locality. 
The complete randomness makes any cache replacement 
policy ineffective; while the lack of spatial locality
makes the notion of ``cache block'' containing 
multiple data items of the basic access granularity seemingly irrelevant.

\xuehai{Our key observation is that
simply ruling out the notion
of ``cache block'' due to randomness is premature, since it sacrifices the 
better read efficiency thanks to cache block, 
which is crucial for achieving good
I/O performance}. 
Higher read bandwidth can be achieved when multiple
data files are fetched in batch.
%instead of being accessed individually through multiple requests.
This claim does have a caveat: the benefit is
only achieved when
all or most of the data items in the ``cache block''
are eventually consumed by the application after the 
whole block is brought to memory.
Otherwise, the data movement in cache block granularity
can actually lead to bandwidth waste.
%We find that this 
%condition can be naturally satisfied with the unique
%property of DLT data access. 




%When the memory capacity is significantly smaller than the dataset size, the effectiveness of these approaches can be insignificant. Given the ever-growing data sizes,
%approaches that can significantly reduce DLT's I/O overhead with limited memory capacity are desirable.


%Most of existing methods of addressing the I/O bottleneck of DLT without changing the randomness of data access~\cite{mohan2021coordl, yang2019locality-aware, dryden2021nopfs} focus on caching a fixed portion of data in memory,  thereby ensuring that the DL framework can read the cached portion of data in every epoch. 
%While these memory management strategies can maintain a constant memory hit rate, their effects are limited by the memory capacity of the computing nodes. Essentially, they establish a partial one-to-one mapping mechanism between the dataset and memory. This means that a portion of the dataset is directly mapped to and cached in memory, while the rest has to be retrieved from the storage. Therefore, these approaches only target accelerating access to a portion of the data. The proportion of data whose access can be accelerated depends entirely on the memory capacity. When the memory capacity is significantly smaller than the dataset size, the effectiveness of these approaches can be insignificant. Given the ever-growing data sizes,
%approaches that can significantly reduce DLT's I/O overhead with limited memory capacity are desirable.

This paper proposes \xuehai{{\em Brand}, a new memory management system for DLT 
with {\em \underline{b}}atched {\em \underline{rand}}om data access in a system setting}
where the memory capacity is 
much smaller than the size of the training datasets.
The general principle is to leverage the ``no fixed accessing order'' property to enable batched data file read
with minimum I/O bandwidth waste. 
\xuehai{Brand} starts with a bold design choice that 
data files are {\em always} read from disk in batch,
named {\em chunk}.
A chunk contains a fixed number (chunk size) of
data files and is determined
before DLT in the initialization
and unchanged across training epochs.
Different chunks contain disjoint sets of data files. 
When a data file is requested, its corresponding chunk
and the index inside the chunk are known.
Since not all the chunks in training dataset can fit
in memory, we keep track of each in-memory chunk by
an {\em abstract chunk}, which contains the \xuehai{{\em pointers}}
to the files of the corresponding chunk (chunk slots).
A group of chunks can be mapped to the same abstract
chunk, such group is called a {\em chunk group}.
This resembles the similarity to the 
cache block and the data in memory:
due to the larger memory size, multiple 
data blocks can be mapped to the same cache line.
All abstract chunks together form the logical
{\em abstract memory}. 
The \xuehai{{\bf key problem}} is how to ensure that the files batched read from disk
into memory can be all eventually consumed by DLT process.

We propose several novel system mechanisms
to achieve this goal.
In \xuehai{Brand}, data files are always read from disk into memory at chunk granularity in batch.
A data file of a chunk in memory invalidates
itself after being consumed by DLT. Thus, an abstract
chunk may have some empty file slots.
Due to the randomness, when a file is access, the
system can choose \xuehai{any} chunk in the corresponding chunk group to memory, which may or may not be the chunk
that actually contains the file according to the
initial file-to-chunk mapping.
Most importantly, 
a chunk {\em never evicts} another chunk in the same
chunk group.
When a file is accessed, we check the abstract chunk
of the file's corresponding chunk group,
if the file's slot (index inside the abstract chunk) 
points to a valid file in memory, then that file is returned.
Returning ``whatever available'' seems to be counter-intuitive, \xuehai{but} due to the inherently random access pattern
for DLT, it is indeed correct. 
In Section~\ref{sec:randomnessDiscussion}, we prove that \xuehai{Brand}'s data access
policy does not affect randomness.

If the file's slot does not point to a valid
data file, the system reads another chunk
in the same chunk group, and fills all invalid slots
in the abstract chunk.
On receiving the fetched chunk,
if a chunk slot (different from the 
requested file's slot) 
points to a valid data file,
or a file is already consumed (indicated by
a {\em filled} bit), these files are not 
filled into the target abstract chunk, leading
to wasted chunk read. 
%The files for the valid slots (or have been consumed, 
%indicated by a {\em filled} bit) are discarded and will
%be accesses sometimes in future. 
%Based on the above procedure, it is important to 
%reduce the wasted chunk read. 
%Since in MemHub, 
%the read is always at chunk granularity, 
%The waste
%occurs when the fetched chunk contains an already
%consumed file (filled=1); or the abstract chunk slot
%is still valid (wait to be consumed). 
%We propose two optimizations to reduce such waste.
We can opportunistically reduce the waste by choosing the chunk from a chunk group
considering its filled bit and the current 
status of the abstract chunk for the chunk group.

The above single-node design of \xuehai{Brand}
can be elegantly extended to distributed
scenario with multiple nodes. 
Similar to \xuehai{distributed} shared memory,
each node has the same abstract memory space,
but each abstract memory location has an owner node. A node can access all files mapped to
all abstract location, but if it is not the owner, it needs to request the data through
the network from the owner.
In this way, the data access policy for 
remote abstract memory is completely 
independent to the local data access.
We propose \xuehai{an} efficient data prefetch algorithm
to reduce miss rate and the number of remote
access. 
Interestingly, prefetching from the owner 
offers the {\em positive side-effects} to
reduce the read waste: the prefetched data
sent to remote node will release more
abstract chunk, so that more data can be 
filled into memory.

\begin{comment}
Moreover, in distributed training, one machine can 
access training data from the remote memory.
Here, prefetching remote files not only reduces
access latency but also has the positive ``side effect''
of releasing the memory of the remote machine, so that
the abstract chunks would have more empty slots to be
filled, therefore, reducing the wasted read. 
MemHub schedules the prefetches \yuhao{ when a node needs to request data from other node in  distributed training}. 
The results show that the two optimizations can 
reduce wasted read by 8\% and 29\%,
respectively, and by 33\% when both applied.
\end{comment}

% \xuehai{WRITE A NEW PARAGRAPH: (1) Summarize the 
% implementation; (2) How did you do the evaluation;
% (3) summarizing the results. }
We implement an open-source prototype of \xuehai{Brand}~\footnote{\url{https://github.com/Brand-Official/Brand}} and integrate it with PyTorch. We conducted extensive experiments using three datasets, multiple DNN models, and three different hardware setups representing scenarios with less and more computing power, respectively. The results indicate that, while ensuring the convergence of model training, \xuehai{Brand} consistently outperforms vanilla PyTorch by up to 4.57 times, with peaks reaching 1.96 times speedup that of related work, particularly under limited memory constraints.

This mechanism can map every random data request to a specific memory location, even when the dataset size far exceeds the memory capacity. It adopts optimized batch data loading from the storage and remote data prefetching from remote nodes in distributed training to fill the memory with valid data for DLT's random data access. In this way, MemHub successfully reduces the memory miss rate of DLT's data access while minimizing I/O overhead. Most importantly, this is achieved without sacrificing any randomness of DL frameworks' data access, thereby not harming the convergence of DNN models.

Based on this scheme, MemHub can maximize memory and I/O efficiency and achieve a better results in addressing the I/O bottleneck of DLT.

\section{Background}
\label{sec:background}
\subsection{DLT's I/O Bottleneck}


When memory capacity is insufficient to cache the training dataset in memory, I/O often becomes the performance bottleneck for DLT,
\xuehai{particularly} due to its random data access pattern. We \xuehai{perform} experiments to measure the I/O overhead of training different models on the ImageNet-1k dataset (135 GB)~\cite{deng2009imagenet}. The experiments are conducted on three nodes, each with one NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU and a memory capacity of 60 GB. We use ``epoch time'' to refer to the time taken to complete one epoch of end-to-end training and ``I/O overhead percentage'' to refer to the percentage of epoch time solely occupied by I/O overhead. The I/O overhead is measured by comparing training time with data read from storage and training time with data dynamically generated by a data generator without any I/O. Further information on the experimental setup can be found in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}.
As shown in Table \ref{tab:overheadOfDataLoading},  the experimental results indicate that in the training of all the models, I/O overhead occupies a significant percentage of epoch time, ranging from 65\% to 91\%.
In the training of ResNet50~\cite{he2016resnet}, a model with heavier computation, the I/O overhead still accounts for 65\% of the training time. Furthermore, for lightweight models such as SqueezeNet~\cite{iandola2016squeezenet}, the I/O overhead is up to 91\%. The I/O overhead can be attributed to the following reasons.

In DLT, the gradient descent algorithm (e.g.,  \textit{stochastic
gradient-descent} (SGD)~\cite{bottou2018sgd}, Adam~\cite{kingma2014adam}, Momentum
~\cite{yu1993Momentum}) is typically run for many epochs to adjust the model's weights and parameters until the model converges. In each epoch, the algorithm goes through the entire dataset once randomly. To do this, popular DL frameworks like PyTorch shuffle the dataset indices at the start of each epoch using a random seed, creating a random access sequence. Then the DL frameworks access data following this random access sequence in this epoch. Each data item will be accessed once at an unpredictable time during each epoch. When the dataset size significantly exceeds the memory capacity, the data access pattern will render classical memory replacement strategies (e.g., LRU, LFU) ineffective in achieving high memory hit rate. 

Training in a distributed setting~\cite{dean2012dedistributedtraining,ben2019dedistributedtraining} amplifies the problem. 
In widely used data parallelism, 
distributed training employs multiple computing nodes to accelerate the training task, where each node is responsible for a part of the training dataset. 
To achieve this, the random access sequence generated at the beginning of an epoch is evenly partitioned into all the nodes. This process makes the data each node reads in each epoch \xuehai{nondeterministic}. In another word, for each node, the data brought to memory in
an epoch may no longer be useful for the subsequent epochs, resulting in an even lower memory hit rate and posing a greater challenge to memory management. 

Furthermore, inputs to DLT are often stored in many small files, which incur \xuehai{higher} I/O overhead \xuehai{than large files} when 
they are randomly accessed.
%and randomly accessing them can incur 
%high I/O overhead. 
To minimize the overhead, large-scale analytics systems~\cite{ghemawat2003gfs,shvachko2010hadoop} typically re-organize them into relatively large data chunks and employ batched reading. However, due to the random access pattern, directly
applying batched reading to DLT is not as effective. 
Specifically, when a chunk of data is loaded from 
external storage, there is no way to ensure that
all or most of the data contained in the chunk are
utilized by the DL framework before being swapped
out of memory.
%reading a data item from external storage, a large chunk of data will be loaded, and they will probably not be accessed by the DL framework before being swapped out of memory. 
This explains why it is challenging for DL frameworks to take advantage of batched reading and why popular frameworks like PyTorch do not employ this technique.


\subsection{Related Work}

%There are some recent studies on addressing DLT's I/O bottleneck addressing some of the aspects mentioned above.

DIESEL+~\cite{wang2021diesel+} aims to alleviate DLT's I/O bottleneck of reading 
small files by batched reading and grouping training data into data chunks to improve performance. To support random data access, shuffling is performed at the chunk
level. 
%a chunk-wise shuffle scheme is introduced where shuffling occurs at the chunk level, with partial shuffling between some chunks. 
However, unlike Brand, DIESEL does not guarantee data randomness across the entire dataset.
Some approaches~\cite{mohan2021coordl, yang2019locality-aware, dryden2021nopfs} aim to optimize memory management by caching a fixed portion of data in memory without eviction. These approaches guarantee that the data cached in memory will be hit once per epoch.
\xuehai{In distributed training, the cached data
can be transferred to remote nodes.
This approach is inherently limited by 
memory capacity}. 
%, unlike traditional strategies (e.g., LRU, LFU). 
%For distributed training, they enable each node to access data cached in the other nodes' memory over the network. This ensures that the data cached in memory on every node can be hit once per epoch during distributed training. These approaches do not alter the random data access pattern. However, they do not address performance issues caused by small file reading, and their effectiveness is limited by the memory capacity. %Frequent read requests of small files on the storage system still incur significant I/O overhead.

Some other approaches~\cite{2018zhudeepio, 2022nguyenPartial-Shuffle} focus on optimizing I/O for distributed training by localized shuffling. They allow each node to independently shuffle locally cached or stored data to alleviate low memory hit rates caused by global shuffling. Additionally, they employ techniques like double buffering and cross-node data sharing to overlap disk I/O. \subsection{MemHub Overview}
MemHub aims to fundamentally address the I/O bottleneck of DLT while maintaining the randomness of its data access. MemHub adopts batch reading to minimize the overhead of reading small files, where data are reorganized into relatively large data chunks as the smallest unit of I/O from the storage. With batch reading, the random data access pattern of DLT has especially low memory and I/O efficiency because every I/O operation loads a lot of data from storage to memory, but most of them will not be utilized by DLT before being swapped out of memory. To address this problem, the gist of Memhub consists of the following two aspects:
\begin{itemize}
    \item MemHub maximizes memory and I/O efficiency by ensuring the DL framework uses every loaded data item before replacing it. When reading a data chunk from storage, MemHub attempts to place its data into specific memory locations. A data item can be filled into a memory location only when that memory location either has no cached data or its cached data has been used by one of the computing nodes.

\item MemHub conducts an N-to-M mapping of the data items to the memory locations. The mapping is done in such a way that the $N$ data items are evenly distributed among the $M$ memory locations of all the computing nodes, with each data item being mapped to exactly one location. Accordingly, the data indices in the random access sequence generated by the DL frameworks are mapped to the memory locations in the same way. However, instead of returning the data with the exact index specified by the random access sequence, MemHub returns a random data item among those mapped to the corresponding memory location, thereby ensuring the data randomness while enhancing I/O efficiency.

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Batch Memory-Filling Mechanism}
\label{sec:batchMemoryFiling}

As mentioned earlier, MemHub uses data chunks as the smallest data loading unit to achieve batch data reading and memory filling. So MemHub has to load a data chunk for memory filling when a memory miss occurs at a memory location. To establish the batch memory-filling mechanism, we need to address three questions:

\textbf{1. How do we fill data chunks into memory?}

Recall that MemHub only ``replaces'' the data cached at a memory location after the DL frameworks have accessed it.
Due to the randomness of data access, we cannot guarantee that all the memory locations a data chunk is mapped to are available for data filling. Instead of requiring all data in a data chunk to be filled into memory at once, MemHub will fill as many as possible. This means a data chunk may be loaded from the storage multiple times within one epoch. When a data item is filled into memory, the "Filled" field of this data in the mapping information (as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:generationOfdataChunksAndMapping}) will be set to \(True\) to prevent it from being redundantly filled into memory again in the same epoch. Based on such chunk filling rules, MemHub does not need to perform eviction replacement on the data that has been filled into memory, because the data mapped to the same memory location is equally important for model training. As long as the data is filled into the memory, it must be required by the model training.



\textbf{2. How do we choose the target data chunk?}

The data chunks to be considered should contain data mapped to the target memory location that has not been filled into memory in the current epoch.  
For example, in Figure~\ref{fig:generationOfdataChunksAndMapping}, when a data request is mapped to \(M0\), if the data \(j\) corresponding to \(M0\) in \(Chunk 1\) has already been filled into memory earlier, then only \(Chunk 0\) and \(Chunk 2\) can fill data into \(M0\) at this moment. 

Furthermore, to optimize performance, it is crucial to minimize MemHub's repeated loading of a data chunk within each epoch. To achieve this, MemHub adopts an optimization algorithm for choosing the data chunk, which is run whenever memory filling is initiated. The algorithm's objective is to ensure data randomness while minimizing the number of times a data chunk is loaded.  


The algorithm adopts a metric called \(fill\_rate\) to guide the choice of the data chunk. \(fill\_rate\) can be calculated as \(fill\_rate=\frac{fillable\_number}{unfilled\_number}\), where \(fillable\_number\) represents the number of memory locations that the data chunk can fill at a particular time and \(unfilled\_number\) represents the remaining number of memory locations yet to be filled by this data chunk, indicating the total amount of data within the chunk that has not been filled into memory. Choosing data chunks with a higher \(fill\_rate\) can fill more data from this chunk into memory, thus reducing the number of repeated reads. In addition, among the chunks with the same \(fill\_rate\), choosing the one with a higher \(fillable\_number\) can fill more memory locations.

MemHub's chunk selection algorithm is shown in Algorithm \ref{algorithm:optimizedChunkSelecting}. This algorithm consists of the following steps. It first selects all the valid chunks from the chunk group and puts them into a random order. A chunk is valid when it has data not yet filled into the target memory location in this epoch. It retrieves all the memory locations that could be mapped to the chunk group but are not currently caching any data, denoted as $fillable\_mem\_locs$. The algorithm iterates through the fillable memory locations for each valid chunk to calculate its \(fillable\_number\) and \(fill\_rate\). Effectively this algorithm chooses the chunk primarily with the highest \(fill\_rate\) and secondarily with the highest \(fillable\_number\) among all the valid chunks. A random selection will be made among those with identical metrics.

In Figure~\ref{fig:batchMemoryFillingUnderDifferentCases} , this paper provides some examples based on the N-to-M mapping mechanism depicted  in Figure~\ref{fig:generationOfdataChunksAndMapping} for different cases. Let's focus on the \(chunk\) \(group0\), which consists of \(chunk 0\), \(chunk 1\), and \(chunk 2\). The corresponding abstract memory locations are \(M0\), \(M1\), and \(M2\). In case (a), suppose the DLT Framework requests data item \(j\) from MemHub. According to the N-to-M mapping mechanism, data item \(j\) will be mapped to M0, which does not cache any data. Therefore, a memory miss occurs, and Algorithm \ref{algorithm:optimizedChunkSelecting} will start working. Since all the data in these three chunks (\(chunk 0\), \(chunk 1\), and \(chunk 2\)) have not been filled into memory during this epoch, the \(fill\_rate\) for all three chunks are 1.0. Algorithm \ref{algorithm:optimizedChunkSelecting} will randomly select one of these chunks as the target chunk to fill into memory. Suppose \(chunk 0\) is randomly selected; then the data items \(c\), \(f\), and \(q\) will be sequentially filled into \(M0\), \(M1\), and \(M2\), respectively. Finally, the MemHub will return the cached data item \(c\) from \(M0\) to the model for training. Similarly, in case (b), the requested data item \(f\) will be mapped to \(M1\), causing a memory miss. At this point, \(chunk 0\) cannot be considered as a candidate chunk since all of its data has already been filled into memory. For \(chunk 1\) and \(chunk 2\), since all of their data has not been filled into memory yet, their \(unfilled\_number\) are 3. However, only \(M0\) and \(M1\) do not have cached data, making the \(fillable\_number\) for the two chunks equal to 2. Therefore, their \(fill\_rate\) are both 0.67. Algorithm \ref{algorithm:optimizedChunkSelecting} will now randomly select one of the two chunks as the target chunk. Suppose \(chunk 2\) is chosen; then the data items \(l\) and \(e\) from \(chunk 2\) will be filled into \(M0\) and \(M1\), respectively, while data item \(o\) will not be filled into memory this time. Afterwards, the cached data item \(e\) in \(M1\) will be returned for training. In case (c), the requested data item \(b\) will be mapped to \(M2\), which also results in a memory miss. At this point, only \(chunk 1\) and \(chunk 2\) can be considered for filling \(M2\). According to the definition of the \(fill\_rate\), we can calculate that the \(fill\_rate\) for \(chunk 1\) is 0.67, while the \(fill\_rate\) for \(chunk 2\) is 1.0. Therefore, \(chunk 2\) will be selected as the target chunk to be filled into memory. In this case, only the data item \(o\) will be filled into \(M2\) and then returned to the model for training.

Once the prefetch buffer's memory space is exhausted, no further allocations are made to remote abstract memory to prevent OOM conditions. Given that MemHub does not permit dropping prefetched data, when a requester requests the sender for data, it simultaneously sends the remaining allocatable memory space \(r\) in its prefetch buffer to the sender. During prefetch execution, the sender takes \(r\) into account, ensuring that the size of the prefetched data does not exceed \(r\). Furthermore, MemHub supports determining the upper limit of the prefetch buffer through hyperparameter search to ensure optimal training performance.}

After the sender provides data as prefetch,

This happens to have positive effects on the

On the left, with no prefetch,
after responding the request, one slot on 
the sender side becomes empty. 
Then a following local batch read will 
be able to fill two entries, leading to 
a \(fill\_rate\) of 67\%.
On the right, with prefetch, the sender
provides one more data, so the later
batch read can achieve

\subsection{Randomness Guarantee}
\label{sec:randomnessDiscussion}
%With the introduction of the data mapping mechanism and the data access protocol in MemHub, we can view the dataset as a two-dimensional data array. One axis of this array represents all abstract memory locations, while the other represents the data mapped to each memory location. Thus, 
%randomly choosing data in MemHub is equivalent to randomly choosing data from this two-dimensional array. Because the data access sequence is randomly generated, the 
%sequence of target memory locations for data access is also random. Therefore, to prove that MemHub's entire data selection process is random, we only need to prove that the data retrieved from a memory location is randomly selected among those mapped to this location. 

\textbf{Lemma.} \textit{When a memory miss occurs, the target chunk is always randomly selected from its chunk group for memory filling.} 


\textbf{Proof.} Assuming that chunk \( x \) is selected for memory filling based on the
local protocol of Brand during a memory miss, and this memory filling is the \( i \)-th filling of chunk \( x \). Based on this assumption, we define the following sets:

\( S \): Set of memory locations mapped by chunk \( x \).

\( M_i \): Set of memory locations in \(S\) not caching data before the \( i \)-th filling of chunk \( x \).

\( U_i \): Set of memory locations in \(S\) never filled by chunk \( x \) before the \( i \)-th filling.

\( F_i \): Set of memory locations in \(S\) filled by chunk \( x \) during it's \( i \)-th filling.

\( S \) is the universal set of \( M_i \), \( U_i \), and \( F_i \), and they have the following relationship: $F_i = M_i \cap U_i$. 
Based on the
local protocol of Brand, the \(fill\_rate_i\) of chunk \( x \) is: 

\[ fill\_rate_i = \frac{fillable\_number_i}{chunk\_size}=\frac{size(F_i)}{chunk\_size}=\frac{size( M_i \cap U_i)}{chunk\_size}\] 

Therefore, \(fill\_rate_i\) is directly influenced by \(M_i\) and \(U_i\). We 
consider the following two cases.

(1) When \(i=1\), chunk \(x\) is randomly selected. This is because for data chunks within the same group that are not yet selected for memory filling, \(U_1\) can be represented as: $U_1 = S$.
Since \(M_1\) and \(S\) are the same for these data chunks, they have identical \(fillable\_number_1\) and \(fill\_rate_1\). Therefore, according to the
local protocol of Brand, chunk \(x\) must be selected randomly from these chunks.

(2) When \(i>1\), according to the definition of \( U_i \), it is actually related to \( U_{i-1} \) and \( F_{i-1} \), as follows:
$U_i = U_{i-1} - F_{i-1}$.
Therefore, 
$U_i = U_{i-1} - M_{i-1} \cap U_{i-1} = (S - M_{i-1}) \cap U_{i-1}$.
Similarly,
$F_i  = M_i \cap (S - M_{i-1}) \cap U_{i-1}$.
Here, \(S\) is independent of chunk \(x\). \( M_i \) represents the set of memory locations that do not cache data when chunk \( x \) is selected for memory filling for the \( i \)-th time. A memory location that does not cache data either because it has not been filled initially or because the data that it cached before has been read based on the random access sequence. So \( M_i \) and \(M_{i-1}\) are independent of the chunk \(x\).

 Hence, \(U_i\) and \(F_i\) only depend on \(U_{i-1}\), meaning that the \(i\)th selection of chunk \(x\) depends only on its \(i-1\)st selection. Following this logic, each subsequent chunk selection depends solely on the previous one. Thus, it can be concluded that the \(i\)th selection of chunk \(x\) depends only on its first selection. Since we have already proved that the first selection of chunk \(x\) is random, it follows that the \(i\)th selection of chunk \(x\) is also random.

Therefore, in Brand, when a memory miss occurs, the target chunk is always randomly selected from its chunk group for memory filling. $\square$ 


\textbf{Theorem.} \textit{DL frameworks using a random sequence of unique data indices to iterate data from Brand can iterate data in a random order.}  

\textbf{Proof.} 
Because each data index in the random access sequence produced by the DL frameworks is random, the memory location that it is mapped to is also random. Furthermore,
based on \textit{Lemma}, the target chunk is always randomly selected from its chunk group for memory filling. It can be inferred that the data filled into a memory location each time is randomly selected among those mapped to this location. Therefore, the data item that is read by Brand is random. $\square$

In this way, MemHub can seamlessly integrate into various popular DL frameworks. In this paper, we integrate MemHub into the DataLoader module of PyTorch. %and the resulting module does not differ much from the native DataLoader of PyTorch. %MemHub only needs to provide a small amount of additional parameters or configuration information.

%MemHub also supports a multi-worker mode to accelerate data loading and processing, leveraging the parallel processing capability of multi-threads. 
The entire implementation of Brand includes two types of modules: multiple clients and a server. A client corresponds to a process, serving as a worker responsible for receiving data indices from the DL frameworks and requesting the target data from the server. The server primarily carries out Brand's core functionalities. In addition, Brand encompasses two communication modules: \textit{Inter-Process Communication} (IPC) for facilitating communication between the client and server within the same node, and notably, gRPC-based communication, a protocol specifically designed for efficient and scalable  \textit{remote procedure calls} (RPC) for cross-node data sharing between the servers. 
%The configuration file states each training node’s IP address and port number to enable cross-node data sharing.

The interaction between Brand and storage is carried out through the abstract interface provided by the OS's virtual file system, and it does not depend on any specific storage. Like ordinary DL frameworks, data accessing can be achieved by simply providing the dataset's root directory with an additional parameter, the size of data chunks. Afterward, data chunks will be automatically generated, validated, and loaded without additional user intervention.

\subsection{Methodology} 

\textbf{Experimental Setup}. 
Our experiments were conducted in three environments, as summarized in Table \ref{tab:experimentSetup}. 
For A10 and P100 setups, each node is equipped with dual Intel Xeon E5-2682 v4 4-core processors. Training data for these two setups is stored on an Apsara File Storage NAS ~\cite{alibabacloud-nas} with a capacity of 10 PB. In contrast, the A100 setup uses nodes equipped with dual AMD EPYC 7402 24-core processors.  Training data for the A100 nodes is stored on a Lustre file system with a capacity of 2 PB. All the servers run on CentOS Linux 7 (Core) with CUDA Toolkit version 11.2, and PyTorch version 1.7.0 is used for the experiments. 

%The first setup, named A10, consists of five nodes, each equipped with one NVIDIA Tesla A10 GPU with 24GB of memory. The second setup, named P100, consists of three nodes, each equipped with one NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU with 16GB of memory. Each node in both the A10 and P100 setups is equipped with dual Intel Xeon E5-2682 v4 4-core processors and 60GB of memory. The network bandwidth for each node in both the A10 and P100 setups is 3 Gb/s, or approximately 0.38 GB/s.

The A100 setup also involves three nodes, each with dual AMD EPYC 7402 24-core processors, 256 GB memory, and four NVIDIA Tesla A100 GPUs with 40 GB memory. The network bandwidth of the A100 nodes is approximately 3 GB/s. Training data for the A100 nodes is stored on a Lustre file system with a capacity of 2 PB. All the servers run on CentOS Linux 7 (Core) with CUDA Toolkit version 11.2, and PyTorch version 1.7.0 is used for the experiments.

\textbf{Workloads}. As shown in Table \ref{tab:workloads}, we evaluate Brand across two domains: \textit{Automatic Speech Recognition} (ASR) and \textit{Computer Vision} (CV). The evaluation involves three datasets of varying sizes and six state-of-the-art models.

For ASR, we validated the Wav2Vec 2.0\cite{baevski2020wav2vec} model on the LibriSpeech\cite{panayotov2015librispeech} dataset using the A10 setup. LibriSpeech is a classic dataset in the field of ASR, consisting of around 1000 hours of 16 kHz recorded English speech. The training set totals around 60 GB, containing 0.28 million audio clips, with an average file size of about 200 kilobytes per clip. Wav2Vec 2.0 is a self-supervised\cite{jaiswal2020self-supervised} model for speech recognition, using a convolutional and transformer\cite{vaswani2017attentionnlp} architecture. 

For CV,  we evaluate Brand across five state-of-the-art deep learning models: SqueezeNet~\cite{iandola2016squeezenet}, MobileNetV3~\cite{howard2017mobilenets}, ResNet50~\cite{he2016resnet}, DenseNet121~\cite{huang2017densenet}, and VGG16~\cite{simonyan2014vggnet}, commonly employed in CV. Our evaluation covers two datasets with distinct sizes: ImageNet-1k~\cite{deng2009imagenet}, containing around 1.2 million images across 1,000 classes, totaling 135 GB, and ImageNet-21k~\cite{deng2009imagenet}, an extension of ImageNet-1k with over 13 million images across 19,167 classes, taking up approximately 1.1 TB. Each dataset's file sizes vary from a few kilobytes to several hundred kilobytes. All evaluations are performed using the specified models on the following hardware configurations: SqueezeNet, MobileNetV3, and ResNet50 on ImageNet-1k are run on A10 and P100, while DenseNet121 and VGG16 on ImageNet-21k are run on A100. 

The batch size is set to maximize GPU utilization. Specifically, for ASR,  Wav2Vec 2.0 use a batch size of 64 on A10. For CV, on A10 and P100, SqueezeNet use a batch size of 512 per GPU, MobileNetV3 uses 256 per GPU, and ResNet50 uses 128 per GPU. For A100, DenseNet121 and VGG16 all use a batch size of 256 per GPU. Furthermore, to accelerate the speed of data loading and preprocessing, the number of parallel threads for the DataLoader will be set based on the 4 workers/GPU principle. The default chunk size in Brand is set to 64 unless specified otherwise.

\textbf{Baselines}.
(1) PyTorch: uses the native PyTorch DataLoader, relying on the operating system's cache policy for memory management.
(2) No-I/O: based on the native PyTorch DataLoader but replaces the I/O reading by randomly simulating training data generation.
This baseline does not incur any I/O cost and represents the upper bound of any optimization.
(3) CoorDL~\cite{mohan2021coordl}: caches fixed data in memory without memory replacement, representing the state-of-the-art approaches without sacrificing data randomness.

\textbf{ImageNet-1k}. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:overallPerformance-imagenet-1k}, to evaluate Brand's performance under different memory and hardware conditions, we conducted two sets of experiments. On the A10 setup, we focused on assessing the distributed performance of Brand in a scenario with limited memory resources. On the P100 setup, we evaluated Brand's performance for both single-node training and distributed training under conditions of ample global memory. When training on three A10 nodes, the global memory can only cache 25\% of ImageNet-1k. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:overallPerformance-threeA10Nodes}, Brand achieves a maximum 2.26x speed improvement over PyTorch and is 1.96x faster than CoorDL in this case. In Figure~\ref{fig:overallPerformance-fiveA10Nodes}, Brand outperforms PyTorch by up to 2.47x and is 1.69x faster than CoorDL when training on five A10 nodes whose global memory can cache about 40\% data. When training on one P100 node, Brand and CoorDL do not perform data sharing across nodes. In this case, Brand outperforms PyTorch by up to 2.13x, and surpasses CoorDL with a maximum speedup of 1.45x as shown in \ref{fig:overallPerformance-oneP100Node}. The last experiment is conducted on three P100 Nodes whose global memory can cache the entire dataset. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:overallPerformance-threeP100Nodes}, the performance of Brand is up to 4.57x that of PyTorch. Thanks to the implementation of Brand's prefetch mechanism, Brand achieves 1.32x better performance compared to CoorDL. Specifically, for GPU-intensive models like ResNet50, the performance of Brand has already caught up with No-I/O, meaning it does not introduce additional I/O overhead.

% 3 A10 nodes, 5 A10 nodes, 1 P100 nodes, and 3 P100 nodes. The global memory in these four environments can cache 25\%, 40\%, 35\%, and 100\% of ImageNet-1k, respectively. In Figure~\ref{fig:overallPerformance-fiveA10Nodes}, MemHub outperforms PyTorch by up to 2.47x  and is 1.69x faster than CoorDL when training on five A10 nodes whose global memory can cache about 40\% data. The performance of CoorDL is directly dependent on the size of the global memory. Therefore, as the global memory increases, the performance gap between CoorDL and MemHub decreases. We tested the performance on the P100 setup with larger global memory.  As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:overallPerformance-twoP100Nodes}, when training on two P100 nodes, the global memory can cache 70\% of the data. The performance of MemHub is up to 2.78x that of PyTorch, and 1.38x that of CoorDL. When training on three P100 nodes, the global memory can cache the entire dataset. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:overallPerformance-threeP100Nodes}, the performance of MemHub is up to 4.57x that of PyTorch. Thanks to the implementation of MemHub's prefetch mechanism, MemHub achieves 1.32x better performance compared to CoorDL. Specifically, for GPU-intensive models like ResNet50, the performance of MemHub has already caught up with No-I/O, meaning it does not introduce additional I/O overhead.}

We evaluate the performance of these two algorithms by training ResNet50 on ImageNet-1k across three A10 nodes and report three key factors: epoch time, memory misses, and remote data requests.

\subsection{Remote Abstract Memory Usage}
\label{sec:prefetch-buffer}

The experiments are conducted on three A10 nodes using ImageNet-1k as the dataset and SqueezeNet as the model. We manually set the memory limit of remote abstract memory on each node to a range from 50 MB to 3 GB for our analysis.

As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:prefetchBufferUsage}, when the memory limit of the remote abstract memory is less than 1.5 GB, increasing this limit leads to a corresponding increase in the usage of remote abstract memory, indicating that more prefetched data are being cached. However, when the limit exceeds 1.5 GB, the usage of remote abstract memory does not show significant increases. This implies that allocating additional memory to the remote abstract memory beyond this point results in wasted memory resources. As indicated in Table~\ref{tab:memory limit-epochTime}, the best performance is achieved when the limit is set to 1.5 GB.
% \yuhao{As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:prefetchBufferUsage}, when the prefetch buffer size is less than or equal to 1GB, the buffer is well-utilized with prefetched data. When the prefetch buffer size exceeds 1GB, the actual occupancy of the prefetch buffer begins to exhibit noticeable fluctuations. When the buffer size is increased to 1.5GB, there are still brief moments (peaks) where the occupancy rate approaches 100\%. However, as the buffer size continues to increase beyond this point, the actual occupancy rate tends to decrease, sometimes falling below 50\%.
% Overall, the actual memory usage also decreases as the buffer size increases excessively. This phenomenon can be attributed to the corresponding reduction in local abstract memory size, which serves as the source for prefetching. As the prefetch buffer size grows too large, it compresses the available space for local abstract memory, thereby limiting the amount of data that can be prefetched and ultimately leading to a lower actual memory footprint of the prefetch buffer.}

\subsection{Data Chunk Size Sensitivity Study}
\label{sec:eveluation-chunkSize}

We evaluate the impact of chunk size on the performance of SqueezeNet trained on three A10 nodes with the Imagenet-1k. We analyze the I/O throughput, average number of times each chunk is loaded, and epoch time with chunk sizes varying from 2 to 256, shown in Figure~\ref{fig:chunkSize-throughputAndAverageAccessTimes} and Figure~\ref{fig:chunkSize-epochTime}. 
We compare these results with native PyTorch training with chunk size being 1. 
%represented by the cases of chunk size being 1 in the same figures. 
In general, we can see that I/O throughput rises with chunk sizes. However, in epoch time does not consistently correlate to I/O throughput; it initially decreases with a larger chunk size but increases slightly when the chunk size is larger than 64. This is because, in Brand, a data chunk may be loaded from storage multiple times within an epoch, and each loading only fills a portion of the data into memory. As chunk size increases, the average number of times each chunk is loaded within an epoch also increases, leading to a net increase in the amount of data loaded from the storage. 
It is why the increase of I/O throughput 
does not always lead to epoch time reduction.
Based on our experiment setting, the chunk size of 64 achieves optimal training epoch time. Thus, we adopt this parameter consistently throughout our evaluation.

\subsection{Analysis of Convergence}
\label{sec:convergence}
To evaluate the impact on model convergence during training, we train ResNet50 on two P100 nodes using the ImageNet-1k, running for 90 epochs until convergence, an approach that represents the current state-of-the-art evaluation for DNN training convergence. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:convergence}, throughout the training process, a consistent alignment in Top-1 Accuracy is observed between Brand and PyTorch. Brand achieves its highest accuracy of 75.63 at epoch 83, while PyTorch reaches its peak accuracy of 75.61 at epoch 89.

\section{CONCLUSION}
\label{sec:conclusion}

This paper propose Brand, a comprehensive memory management system for deep learning training (DLT).
In Brand, data files are always read from disk in batch.
Based on this bold assumption, we propose efficient
data access protocol in both single-node
setting and distributed environment with multiple
nodes. 
The protocol minimizes the wasted data read
due to larger granularity, enables efficient
inter-node prefetching, while still ensuring 
randomness required by DLT. The experimental results indicate that Brand can significantly accelerate data fetching in DLT, achieving up to a 4.57x improvement in training time compared to PyTorch.

%While the continuously expanding dataset provides opportunities for the rapid evolution of DNN applications,  it also imposes significant I/O pressure for DLT prioritize random access, particularly when facing limited memory resources. In this paper, we propose MemHub, aiming to improve the I/O performance of DLT while maintaining the randomness of data access based on N-to-M dataset-memory mapping and batch memory-filling. In MemHub, any data random request from the DL framework will be mapped to a special memory location for randomly data accessing, maintaining the randomness of data access. For any memory location, new data is read and replaces the cached data based on batch reading only when the cached data has been used by the DL framework, maximizing memory and I/O efficiency. For distributed training, optimized remote data reading and data prefetching method are implemented to reduce both the storage I/O and the network I/O. We have conducted experiments to evaluate MemHub's performance, and the results demonstrate that, MemHub achieves a performance improvement of up to 4.57x compared to native PyTorch.

%In the future, we plan to research two extensions to further enhance the performance of MemHub. First, our experiments (Section~\ref{sec:eveluation-differentMemoryCapacity}) have revealed that MemHub's performance is slightly inferior to that of CoorDL where the collective memory across the computing nodes is larger than the size of the dataset. This happens because MemHub still needs to perform storage I/O, whereas CoorDL can cache all the data in memory. While MemHub was mainly designed for scenarios with limited memory, there is room to improve its performance when the collective memory of multiple nodes is ample. MemHub's limitation under this scenario is due to the fact that MemHub mainly uses the extra memory on each node to cache prefetched data to reduce network I/O instead of collectively caching more data to reduce storage I/O. We plan to research this optimization to find the optimized trade-off between minimizing the two types of I/Os.

%In the overall design of MemHub, we have already implemented measures such as batch reading and the optimized chunk selection algorithm to optimize its disk I/O. Therefore, for distributed training, MemHub does not undergo specific disk I/O optimization but rather focuses more on reducing remote data requests based on the network through mechanisms like prefetching. This is crucial for distributed training, as confirmed by our experimental results in Section \ref{sec:eveluation-breakdownsAnalysis}, yet this aspect has not been addressed in other related works. However,  Hence, experimental results in Section \ref{sec:eveluation-differentMemoryCapacity} indicate that MemHub's performance is slightly inferior to CoorDL. In summary, there is still room for further optimization of MemHub's disk I/O, especially in distributed training scenarios where the collective memory across all nodes is ample, and this will be our focus in future work.

%Second, in Section~\ref{sec:eveluation-chunkSize}, we evaluate the impact of chunk size on the performance in MemHub. The results indicate that the overall training performance does not necessarily improve with larger chunk size. Instead, there exists a chunk size that can achieve an optimal trade-off between I/O throughput and the repetition of chunk loading. Currently, MemHub requires user intervention in the determination of the chunk size through testing. Enabling automatic tuning of optimal chunk size, for example, through a hyperparameter search, is part of our future plans. Moreover, larger chunk sizes show improved throughput in experimental data. Hence, optimizing MemHub's performance by minimizing the number of times each chunk is loaded with larger chunk sizes is another direction in our research agenda.

title: Data Sharing with a Generative AI Competitor
summary:
As GenAI platforms grow, their dependence on content from competing
providers, combined with access to alternative data sources, creates new
challenges for data-sharing decisions. In this paper, we provide a model of
data sharing between a content creation firm and a GenAI platform that can also
acquire content from third-party experts. The interaction is modeled as a
Stackelberg game: the firm first decides how much of its proprietary dataset to
share with GenAI, and GenAI subsequently determines how much additional data to
acquire from external experts. Their utilities depend on user traffic, monetary
transfers, and the cost of acquiring additional data from external experts. We
characterize the unique subgame perfect equilibrium of the game and uncover a
surprising phenomenon: The firm may be willing to pay GenAI to share the firm's
own data, leading to a costly data-sharing equilibrium. We further characterize
the set of Pareto improving data prices, and show that such improvements occur
only when the firm pays to share data. Finally, we study how the price can be
set to optimize different design objectives, such as promoting firm data
sharing, expert data acquisition, or a balance of both. Our results shed light
on the economic forces shaping data-sharing partnerships in the age of GenAI,
and provide guidance for platforms, regulators and policymakers seeking to
design effective data exchange mechanisms.

title: The Singapore Consensus on Global AI Safety Research Priorities
summary:
Rapidly improving AI capabilities and autonomy hold significant promise of
transformation, but are also driving vigorous debate on how to ensure that AI
is safe, i.e., trustworthy, reliable, and secure. Building a trusted ecosystem
is therefore essential -- it helps people embrace AI with confidence and gives
maximal space for innovation while avoiding backlash.
  The "2025 Singapore Conference on AI (SCAI): International Scientific
Exchange on AI Safety" aimed to support research in this space by bringing
together AI scientists across geographies to identify and synthesise research
priorities in AI safety. This resulting report builds on the International AI
Safety Report chaired by Yoshua Bengio and backed by 33 governments. By
adopting a defence-in-depth model, this report organises AI safety research
domains into three types: challenges with creating trustworthy AI systems
(Development), challenges with evaluating their risks (Assessment), and
challenges with monitoring and intervening after deployment (Control).

title: Modular Counting CSP: Reductions and Algorithms
summary:
The Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) is ubiquitous in various areas of
mathematics and computer science. Many of its variations have been studied
including the Counting CSP, where the goal is to find the number of solutions
to a CSP instance. The complexity of finding the exact number of solutions of a
CSP is well understood (Bulatov, 2013, and Dyer and Richerby, 2013) and the
focus has shifted to other variations of the Counting CSP such as counting the
number of solutions modulo an integer. This problem has attracted considerable
attention recently. In the case of CSPs based on undirected graphs Bulatov and
Kazeminia (STOC 2022) obtained a complexity classification for the problem of
counting solutions modulo p for arbitrary prime p. In this paper we report on
the progress made towards a similar classification for the general CSP, not
necessarily based on graphs.
  We identify several features that make the general case very different from
the graph case such as a stronger form of rigidity and the structure of
automorphisms of powers of relational structures. We provide a solution
algorithm in the case p=2 that works under some additional conditions and prove
the hardness of the problem under some assumptions about automorphisms of the
powers of the relational structure. We also reduce the general CSP to the case
that only uses binary relations satisfying strong additional conditions.

title: LLM-as-a-Judge for Reference-less Automatic Code Validation and Refinement for Natural Language to Bash in IT Automation
summary:
In an effort to automatically evaluate and select the best model and improve
code quality for automatic incident remediation in IT Automation, it is crucial
to verify if the generated code for remediation action is syntactically and
semantically correct and whether it can be executed correctly as intended.
There are three approaches: 1) conventional methods use surface form similarity
metrics (token match, exact match, etc.) which have numerous limitations, 2)
execution-based evaluation focuses more on code functionality based on
pass/fail judgments for given test-cases, and 3) LLM-as-a-Judge employs LLMs
for automated evaluation to judge if it is a correct answer for a given problem
based on pre-defined metrics. In this work, we focused on enhancing
LLM-as-a-Judge using bidirectional functionality matching and logic
representation for reference-less automatic validation and refinement for Bash
code generation to select the best model for automatic incident remediation in
IT Automation. We used execution-based evaluation as ground-truth to evaluate
our LLM-as-a-Judge metrics. Results show high accuracy and agreement with
execution-based evaluation (and up to 8% over baseline). Finally, we built
Reflection code agents to utilize judgments and feedback from our evaluation
metrics which achieved significant improvement (up to 24% increase in accuracy)
for automatic code refinement.

title: Is OpenAlex Suitable for Research Quality Evaluation and Which Citation Indicator is Best?
summary:
This article compares (1) citation analysis with OpenAlex and Scopus, testing
their citation counts, document type/coverage and subject classifications and
(2) three citation-based indicators: raw counts, (field and year) Normalised
Citation Scores (NCS) and Normalised Log-transformed Citation Scores (NLCS).
Methods (1&2): The indicators calculated from 28.6 million articles were
compared through 8,704 correlations on two gold standards for 97,816 UK
Research Excellence Framework (REF) 2021 articles. The primary gold standard is
ChatGPT scores, and the secondary is the average REF2021 expert review score
for the department submitting the article. Results: (1) OpenAlex provides
better citation counts than Scopus and its inclusive document
classification/scope does not seem to cause substantial field normalisation
problems. The broadest OpenAlex classification scheme provides the best
indicators. (2) Counterintuitively, raw citation counts are at least as good as
nearly all field normalised indicators, and better for single years, and NCS is
better than NLCS. (1&2) There are substantial field differences. Thus, (1)
OpenAlex is suitable for citation analysis in most fields and (2) the major
citation-based indicators seem to work counterintuitively compared to quality
judgements. Field normalisation seems ineffective because more cited fields
tend to produce higher quality work, affecting interdisciplinary research or
within-field topic differences.

title: FlexiAct: Towards Flexible Action Control in Heterogeneous Scenarios
summary:
Action customization involves generating videos where the subject performs
actions dictated by input control signals. Current methods use pose-guided or
global motion customization but are limited by strict constraints on spatial
structure, such as layout, skeleton, and viewpoint consistency, reducing
adaptability across diverse subjects and scenarios. To overcome these
limitations, we propose FlexiAct, which transfers actions from a reference
video to an arbitrary target image. Unlike existing methods, FlexiAct allows
for variations in layout, viewpoint, and skeletal structure between the subject
of the reference video and the target image, while maintaining identity
consistency. Achieving this requires precise action control, spatial structure
adaptation, and consistency preservation. To this end, we introduce RefAdapter,
a lightweight image-conditioned adapter that excels in spatial adaptation and
consistency preservation, surpassing existing methods in balancing appearance
consistency and structural flexibility. Additionally, based on our
observations, the denoising process exhibits varying levels of attention to
motion (low frequency) and appearance details (high frequency) at different
timesteps. So we propose FAE (Frequency-aware Action Extraction), which, unlike
existing methods that rely on separate spatial-temporal architectures, directly
achieves action extraction during the denoising process. Experiments
demonstrate that our method effectively transfers actions to subjects with
diverse layouts, skeletons, and viewpoints. We release our code and model
weights to support further research at
https://shiyi-zh0408.github.io/projectpages/FlexiAct/

title: Leveraging Large Language Model for Intelligent Log Processing and Autonomous Debugging in Cloud AI Platforms
summary:
With the increasing complexity and rapid expansion of the scale of AI systems
in cloud platforms, the log data generated during system operation is massive,
unstructured, and semantically ambiguous, which brings great challenges to
fault location and system self-repair. In order to solve this problem, this
paper proposes an intelligent log processing and automatic debugging framework
based on Large Language Model (LLM), named Intelligent Debugger (LLM-ID). This
method is extended on the basis of the existing pre-trained Transformer model,
and integrates a multi-stage semantic inference mechanism to realize the
context understanding of system logs and the automatic reconstruction of fault
chains. Firstly, the system log is dynamically structured, and the unsupervised
clustering and embedding mechanism is used to extract the event template and
semantic schema. Subsequently, the fine-tuned LLM combined with the multi-round
attention mechanism to perform contextual reasoning on the log sequence to
generate potential fault assumptions and root cause paths. Furthermore, this
paper introduces a reinforcement learning-based policy-guided recovery planner,
which is driven by the remediation strategy generated by LLM to support dynamic
decision-making and adaptive debugging in the cloud environment. Compared with
the existing rule engine or traditional log analysis system, the proposed model
has stronger semantic understanding ability, continuous learning ability and
heterogeneous environment adaptability. Experiments on the cloud platform log
dataset show that LLM-ID improves the fault location accuracy by 16.2%, which
is significantly better than the current mainstream methods

title: SECQUE: A Benchmark for Evaluating Real-World Financial Analysis Capabilities
summary:
We introduce SECQUE, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating large language
models (LLMs) in financial analysis tasks. SECQUE comprises 565 expert-written
questions covering SEC filings analysis across four key categories: comparison
analysis, ratio calculation, risk assessment, and financial insight generation.
To assess model performance, we develop SECQUE-Judge, an evaluation mechanism
leveraging multiple LLM-based judges, which demonstrates strong alignment with
human evaluations. Additionally, we provide an extensive analysis of various
models' performance on our benchmark. By making SECQUE publicly available, we
aim to facilitate further research and advancements in financial AI.

title: Task-parallelism in SWIFT for heterogeneous compute architectures
summary:
This paper highlights the first steps towards enabling graphics processing
unit (GPU) acceleration of the smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) solver for
cosmology SWIFT and creating a hydrodynamics solver capable of fully leveraging
the hardware available on heterogeneous exascale machines composed of central
and graphics processing units (CPUs and GPUs). Exploiting the existing
task-based parallelism in SWIFT, novel combinations of algorithms are presented
which enable SWIFT to function as a truly heterogeneous software leveraging
CPUs for memory-bound computations concurrently with GPUs for compute-bound
computations in a manner which minimises the effects of CPU-GPU communication
latency. These algorithms are validated in extensive testing which shows that
the GPU acceleration methodology is capable of delivering up to 3.5x speedups
for SWIFTs SPH hydrodynamics computation kernels when including the time
required to prepare the computations on the CPU and unpack the results on the
CPU. Speedups of 7.5x are demonstrated when not including the CPU data
preparation and unpacking times. Whilst these measured speedups are
substantial, it is shown that the overall performance of the hydrodynamic
solver for a full simulation when accelerated on the GPU of state-of-the-art
superchips, is only marginally faster than the code performance when using the
Grace Hopper superchips fully parallelised CPU capabilities. This is shown to
be mostly due to excessive fine-graining of the tasks prior to offloading on
the GPU. Fine-graining introduces significant over-heads associated with task
management on the CPU hosting the simulation and also introduces un-necessary
duplication of CPU-GPU communications of the same data.

title: Constant-Memory Strategies in Stochastic Games: Best Responses and Equilibria
summary:
(Here is a short version, see our paper for the complete abstract.)
  In this work, we comprehensively investigate the concept of constant-memory
strategies in stochastic games. We first establish some results on best
responses and Nash equilibria for behavioral constant-memory strategies,
followed by a discussion on the computational hardness of best responding to
mixed constant-memory strategies. Those theoretic insights later empower a
generative framework for studying generalizability of single-agent RL
algorithms.

\begin{abstract}
Stochastic games have become a prevalent framework for studying long-term multi-agent interactions, especially in the domain of multi-agent reinforcement learning.
However, the notion of equilibria in a stochastic game is fraught with subtleties, mainly because a strategy in a stochastic game can potentially map any observed history to (possibly randomized) actions, leading to an infinitely large strategy space for each agent.
In particular, it has been proven that there exists a Nash equilibrium implemented by a profile of stationary strategies.
This existence result has largely drawn the community's attention to devising multi-agent learning algorithms to reach a stationary equilibrium.
Nevertheless, in real-world scenarios, particularly when one has only limited knowledge of her opponents, the assumption that all opponents will use stationary strategies is indeed too strong.
To this end, in this paper, we comprehensively investigate a less restricted class of strategies called \textit{constant-memory strategies}, which map constant-length history segments to actions.
Despite being weaker than Turing-machine strategies, constant-memory strategies can lead to better outcomes than those under stationary strategies.
We show that given a constant-memory strategy, there always exists a deterministic constant-memory strategy that uses the same length of memory as a pure strategy best response.
In addition, we provide an existence result for equilibria, indicating that given any finite length of memory, there always exists a Nash equilibrium in which all agents adopt constant-memory strategies using that length of memory.
%It naturally follows that any equilibrium that can be implemented by strategies using memories of a smaller length can also be implemented by strategies using longer memories.
%Thus, employing longer memories implies richer and potentially better outcomes.
However, we also show that the best response against a mixed constant-memory strategy, as if an agent is in a tournament with known opponent types, is not constant-memory and is even hard to compute.
Finally, based on the aforementioned theoretical takeaways, we present simple parameterized methods to generate single-agent RL environments that can be arbitrarily difficult to learn, achievable through slight modifications of the original multi-agent environment.
We hope this work significantly deepens the understanding of theoretical issues in single-agent planning under multi-agent systems and uncovers the connection between decision models in single-agent scenarios and those in multi-agent scenarios.
\\

\textbf{Keywords:} 
Stochastic games; Bounded rationality; Best response; Restricted memory; Reinforcement learning
\end{abstract}

\newpage

\section{Introduction}

% real-world examples modelled by stochastic games; indeed POSG is more general, but SG is a good starting point.
Various real-world situations that involve long-term interactions among a group of participants can be modeled as stochastic games, such as negotiation between multiple stakeholders~\cite{baarslag2016learning, de2017negotiating, baarslag2024multi}, bidding and mechanism design in repeated auctions~\cite{iyer2014mean, balseiro2015repeated, guo2019learning, guo2024generative, su2024auctionnet, shen2020reinforcement}, multi-agent teamwork~\cite{sharon2015conflict, mirsky2022survey, stern2019multi-overview}, and even human-robot collaboration~\cite{zhangbuilding, puig2023habitat}.
Stochastic games, also known as Markov games, model the interactions of these multi-agent systems as  a Markov chain over a set of states, where the transitions are triggered by joint actions and are potentially stochastic.


% 1. some existing result of stochastic games
% 2. some current usage of the above existence result under stationary policies: MARL, opponent modelling
The formalization of stochastic games was first proposed in Shapley's seminal work~\cite{shapley1953stochastic}.
A perfectly rational agent in a stochastic game is supposed to make use of all past histories to determine the next action, and therefore, the notion of strategies, defined as mappings from all possible histories to actions, is inherently complex.
The fact that there are infinitely many strategies prohibits the direct application of Nash's theorem for establishing any existence result of equilibria.
However, the stationary transitions of stochastic games inevitably draw attention to a highly special subclass of time-independent and memoryless strategies that only consider the current states while discarding all past histories, termed \textit{stationary strategies}.
Indeed, the existence of equilibria formed by stationary strategies in 
$n$-player general-sum stochastic games was later proven by~\citeauthor{fink1964equilibrium}~\cite{fink1964equilibrium} and~\citeauthor{takahashi1964equilibrium}~\cite{takahashi1964equilibrium}, under mild assumptions.
Despite being highly restricted in terms of expressiveness, the notion of stationary strategies has enabled the community to practically investigate some complex real-world applications, particularly by resorting to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) techniques, as advocated by~\citeauthor{littman1994markov}~\cite{littman1994markov} and implemented in a line of subsequent work~\cite{lowe2017multi, foerster2018counterfactual, rashid2020monotonic, yu2022the}.


% 1. Some attempt beyond stationary memories in repeated games such as Turing machines / finite automata / constant-memory, mostly under IPD.
% 2. Significance of constant memory strategies, like RNN/Transformers
Notably, one would naturally expect strategies in other less restricted forms that can encode a broader class of behavioral patterns, hoping to achieve better payoff outcomes.
For example, in the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD), if only stationary strategies are considered, there is a unique Nash equilibrium where both players choose \textit{Defect} all the time, resulting in the lowest overall payoff.
However, even with the ability to remember only one past action played by the opponent, the well-known \textit{Tit-For-Tat} (TFT) strategy (having \textit{Cooperate} played in the first step) can be devised.
One can easily see that if both players adopt the TFT strategy, they will follow a trajectory of both playing \textit{Cooperate} throughout the game, resulting in a Nash equilibrium with the highest possible payoff.
%One may additionally note that the proof of the \textit{Folk theorem}~\cite{shoham2008multiagent} (under the average-payoff criterion) also makes use of a combination of a K-cycle strategy together with a Grim trigger.
Apart from other forms of representation, such as strategies represented as finite automata~\cite{rubinstein1986finite, ben1990complexity, zuo2015optimal} and even Turing machines~\cite{megiddo1986play, knoblauch1994computable, nachbar1996non, chen2017bounded},
we focus our main effort on investigating the notion of \textit{constant-memory strategies}, i.e., mappings from history segments of bounded lengths to actions, mainly because it directly relates to the concept of bounded rationality~\cite{simon1990bounded} in general,
and is highly implementable using function approximators like Recurrent Neural Networks~\cite{hochreiter1997long, cho2014learning} and Transformers~\cite{vaswani2017attention} in practice.

%\textcolor{red}{assuming opponents are in constant memory strategies, learned somewhere else}


In this paper, we comprehensively study the theoretical properties associated with \textit{constant-memory strategies}.
We begin by presenting the following two results:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item \textit{A Characterization of Best Responses:} Given a constant-memory strategy profile adopted by the opponents, there always exists a deterministic constant-memory strategy that makes use of the same length of memory acting as a pure strategy best response.
	\item \textit{An Existence Result of Equilibria:} Given any finite length of memory, there always exists a Nash equilibrium where all agents adopt constant-memory (but not necessarily deterministic) strategies using that length of memory.
\end{enumerate}
As a side benefit of using memories of constant length, any strategy that uses a shorter memory can always be implemented by one that uses a longer memory.
Therefore, the above two results directly imply that any NE formed by shorter-length-memory strategies can be transformed into an NE formed by longer-length-memory strategies, suggesting that the longer the memory used by the strategies, the richer the equilibria one can potentially expect.

Additionally, we provide further results about best responses against mixed strategies, mathematically defined as those sampled from a set of support strategies with certain probabilities.
This is associated with broad applications in the domain of opponent modeling~\cite{carmel1998explore, albrecht2015game, albrecht2018autonomous, zhu2025single}, particularly for type-based methods~\cite{albrecht2015game, albrecht2019convergence, albrecht2016belief, zhu2025single}.
However, we demonstrate that:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item \textit{An Negative Result on Strategy Equivalence:} An opponent with a mixed constant-memory strategy may not correspond to an equivalent opponent with a single (behavioral) constant-memory strategy in terms of achieving the same payoff.
	\item \textit{A Negative Result on Best Responses:} The best response against a mixed constant-memory strategy is not necessarily constant-memory, and computing such best responses is computationally hard.
\end{enumerate}

Finally, we translate the aforementioned theoretical insights into a simple generative framework to instantiate single-agent learning environments that can be arbitrarily difficult to learn a good policy.
This, in turn, reveals the potential sources of hardness underlying some single-agent decision-making problems.
